short: Ordered matrix removal is not polynomial

title.title: Polynomial removal fails for ordered binary matrices
title.subtitle: Claim: one fixed $66 \times 66$ zero–one pattern has no polynomial ordered removal bound

plain: Hunt a pattern in a grid of 0s and 1s: a grid can be far from clean, yet hold very few copies

panels.caption: the $2 \times 2$ core of the pattern; the full pattern is $66 \times 66$

beats.text: Ordered copies keep the row and column order, and match zeros as well as ones
Conjecture: a matrix far from pattern-free holds polynomially many copies
The claim: avoidance runs a 1 and a 0 down a binary tree until they collide

steps: Index rows and columns by the leaves of a binary tree
An anchor block forces any copy into fixed roles
A small core pushes a 1 and a 0 down until they collide

data.result: far from free, yet few copies

achievement.label: Polynomial ordered matrix removal (Alon–Ben-Eliezer)
statement: N_H(A) \ge c\,\varepsilon^{C} n^{132} \ \text{ for all far } A
achievement.context: One explicit pattern; whether small patterns admit polynomial removal is open

verify.detail: An explicit $66 \times 66$ pattern defeats every $c, C > 0$; listed
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statement; we did not build it

voice.text: A grid of zeros and ones, far from pattern free. Must it hold many copies?
Rows and columns form a tree; a one and a zero collide at leaves.
Claimed: copies can be extremely rare.

sources.quote: There is an explicit 66x66 binary pattern H
the 2x2 core [[1,0],[1,1]] makes avoidance propagate a 1 and a 0 down tree paths until they collide at the leaves
whether small patterns admit polynomial removal is open
